subject: community-medicine
title: Food Hygiene: Milk Pasteurisation, Phosphatase Test and Egg Quality

steps.title: Milk composition and nutritional profile
steps.tx: Serving as an almost complete physiological food for infant growth, the **nutritional milk composition** provides high biological value casein and whey proteins, emulsified fat droplets, lactose disaccharide, calcium, phosphorus, and riboflavin. However, cow and buffalo milk are notoriously deficient in two essential nutrients: iron and vitamin C (ascorbic acid), meaning infants exclusively fed animal milk beyond six months inevitably develop microcytic iron deficiency anaemia.
steps.say: Milk provides high-quality protein, calcium and B vitamins, but it completely lacks iron and vitamin C. Babies fed cow milk without solids develop severe iron deficiency anaemia.

steps.tx: Labelled pouches of toned and double toned milk still share the nutritional gaps of whole animal milk. **Nutritional milk composition** includes casein and whey of high biological value, emulsified fat, lactose, calcium, phosphorus, and riboflavin. Cow and buffalo milk are poor in iron and in vitamin C. An infant fed only animal milk beyond six months, without other foods, develops microcytic anaemia from iron deficiency. Toning changes the fat. It does not supply the missing iron.
steps.say: Milk supplies high quality protein, fat, lactose, calcium, and riboflavin, but almost no iron or vitamin C. Reducing the fat to make toned milk does not repair that gap. Infants kept on animal milk alone become iron deficient.

steps.title: Milk-borne disease transmission risks
steps.tx: Because raw unpasteurised milk serves as an ideal microbial culture medium, consuming raw dairy carries severe **milk-borne infection hazards**, acquiring pathogens either directly from diseased dairy animals or through unhygienic human handling. Bovine tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium bovis, undulant brucellosis, Q fever, salmonellosis, campylobacter enteritis, listeriosis, and staphylococcal enterotoxin food poisoning spread efficiently through pooled raw milk supplies.
steps.say: Raw milk transmits bovine tuberculosis, brucellosis, Q fever, salmonella and listeria. Drinking unboiled dairy risks chronic fevers and dangerous intestinal infections.

rows: Infected cow udder, mastitis, systemic bovine illness
Milker skin boils, unsterilised milk cans

steps.title: Principles of milk pasteurisation
steps.tx: Developed by Louis Pasteur, **commercial milk pasteurisation** is a thermal process that heats every particle of milk to a specific temperature and holds it for a specific duration, followed by immediate rapid cooling to below five degrees Celsius. The thermal exposure is mathematically calibrated to destroy the most heat-resistant non-spore-forming vegetative pathogen known to be transmitted through milk, namely Coxiella burnetii and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
steps.say: Pasteurisation heats milk to a precise temperature to destroy all disease-causing bacteria, particularly Coxiella and tuberculosis bacilli, before rapidly chilling it below five degrees.

nodes.label: Precise heat holding kills vegetative pathogens
Immediate rapid chilling to < 5 degrees Celsius
Sterile cold packaging in tamper-evident pouches

steps.title: The Holder method: batch pasteurisation
steps.tx: In smaller dairy plants and batch processing facilities, milk is pasteurised using the **Holder method batch technique**, also termed low-temperature long-time pasteurisation (LTLT). Raw milk is placed in a jacketed vat, heated uniformly to not less than sixty-three degrees Celsius (one hundred and forty-five degrees Fahrenheit), held at that precise temperature for at least thirty consecutive minutes, and immediately chilled to five degrees Celsius.
steps.say: The Holder batch method heats milk in a tank to sixty-three degrees Celsius, holds it there for thirty minutes, and chills it immediately. It is ideal for small local dairies.

steps.tx: Plate exchangers move milk across hot metal, which is continuous industrial pasteurisation. Smaller plants still use the **Holder method batch technique**, also called low temperature long time treatment. Raw milk in a jacketed vat is heated evenly to not less than 63 degrees Celsius and held there for at least 30 minutes. It is then chilled at once to 5 degrees Celsius. The half hour hold, not the appearance of the steel, is what defines that batch method.
steps.say: Large plants often use plate heaters. The Holder batch method, used in smaller dairies, heats milk in a vat to at least 63 degrees Celsius, holds it for 30 minutes, and cools it immediately to 5 degrees.

vis.alt: Stainless steel plate heat exchangers fill a commercial milk pasteurisation plant.
vis.caption: Banks of plate heat exchangers heat and cool milk continuously inside a commercial pasteurisation plant. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: High-temperature short-time (HTST) pasteurisation
steps.tx: Modern industrial dairies universally deploy the **HTST continuous pasteurisation** process, passing a continuous thin film of milk between corrugated stainless steel heat exchanger plates. Milk is heated rapidly to at least seventy-two degrees Celsius (one hundred and sixty-one degrees Fahrenheit), held in an insulated holding tube for precisely fifteen seconds, and diverted through regenerative cooling plates directly to refrigerated packaging lines.
steps.say: Large dairies pump milk through hot steel plates at seventy-two degrees Celsius for fifteen seconds. The continuous flow method saves time and energy while killing all germs.

nodes.label: Continuous flow through heat exchanger plates
Heated to 72 degrees C (161 F) for 15 seconds
Flow diversion valve recirculates under-heated milk
Regenerative rapid chilling to 4 degrees C

steps.title: Phosphatase test for pasteurisation verification
steps.tx: The statutory biochemical test verifying adequate pasteurisation is the **standard phosphatase test**, exploiting the enzyme alkaline phosphatase naturally present in raw milk. Because alkaline phosphatase is slightly more heat-resistant than Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Coxiella burnetii, its complete thermal denaturation confirms that all bacterial pathogens have been eradicated; detecting residual phosphatase proves under-pasteurisation or post-process raw milk leakage.
steps.say: The phosphatase test checks whether milk was heated properly. Because alkaline phosphatase resists heat slightly more than tuberculosis bacteria, destroying the enzyme proves the milk is safe.

nodes.label: Alkaline phosphatase present in raw milk

steps.title: Methylene blue and standard plate count tests
steps.tx: To evaluate bacteriological quality before and after processing, dairy laboratories perform the **methylene blue reduction test**, adding methylene blue dye to raw milk and incubating at thirty-seven degrees Celsius. Active bacterial multiplication consumes oxygen, reducing the blue dye to colourless leucomethylene blue; milk that retains its blue color for five hours or longer is graded superior, whereas rapid decolourisation under two hours denotes heavy contamination.
steps.say: Bacteria consume oxygen and bleach methylene blue dye. High-quality clean milk keeps its blue color for over five hours, whereas dirty milk bleaches the dye within two hours.

rows: Moderate bacterial load; acceptable for processing

steps.title: Egg structure and nutritional value
steps.tx: Regarded as a biological reference protein, the **nutritional egg profile** delivers six grams of high biological value protein, five grams of emulsified lipids, bioavailable iron, vitamin A, vitamin D, vitamin B12, and lutein. The yolk concentrates fat and cholesterol, while the egg white (albumen) supplies pure ovalbumin, conalbumin and lysozyme; avidin in raw egg white binds biotin tightly, though heat cooking denatures avidin completely.
steps.say: A single egg supplies six grams of perfect reference protein, vitamin D and choline. Cooking destroys avidin in egg white, preventing it from binding and blocking biotin absorption.

right.title: Egg yolk (Vitellus)
points: Rich in vitamins A, D, B12 and choline

steps.title: Egg candling, freshness and Salmonella enteritidis
steps.tx: Freshness of commercial eggs is evaluated through **optical egg candling**, holding the egg before a bright beam of light in a darkened room to inspect air cell depth, yolk mobility and internal blood spots; fresh eggs exhibit an air cell depth under three millimetres. Furthermore, raw or undercooked eggs pose serious risk of Salmonella enteritidis food poisoning due to transovarian infection, mandating thorough cooking until both yolk and white solidify.
steps.say: Candling holds an egg over a light beam to check the air cell size and freshness. Always cook eggs until firm to kill Salmonella bacteria that can lurk inside raw yolks.

rows: Tiny air cell (< 3 mm depth); central stable yolk
Enlarged air cell (> 6 mm); movable displaced yolk
Sinks to bottom and lies flat on its side
Stands upright or floats to surface (air expansion)
Thick, raised albumen; rounded dome-shaped yolk
Watery, spreading albumen; flattened broken yolk
